title: The Short-Term Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Employment: Evidence from an Online Labor Market
author: Xiang Hui · Oren Reshef · Luofeng Zhou

sib.t: Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market
The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on the Labor Market

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI writing: Present gains can weaken future judgment
st.an: The source establishes that writing is a readily applicable and highly exposed domain for near-term GPT use, particularly for directly reviewable tasks such as copy-editing. It does not assess whether AI-assisted writing weakens future judgment, creates developmental losses, raises substantial verification costs, or requires independent competence assessment, so its position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.
qs: Though similar to other general-purpose technologies, ChatGPT has the potential to transform multiple industries in the long term (Helpman and Trajtenberg, 1994; Eloundou et al., 2023), the tangibility of tasks in the writing industry allows for a straightforward application of GPT’s text-generation capabilities even in the the short term.
For example, users who are looking for copy- editing services can easily copy and paste paragraphs into the GPT prompt and immediately evaluate its output.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Provides direct short-run labour-market evidence that complements the synthesis’s caution against inferring employment outcomes from task-level productivity studies. Its worker-level heterogeneity analysis materially extends the cluster by suggesting adverse effects may vary within occupations and may disproportionately affect higher-quality workers, complicating any assumption that displacement risk is concentrated only among juniors or lower-skilled workers. Its online-freelance setting does not establish a general or legal-sector effect.
qs: 2    Heterogeneous Treatment Effects  Having documented robust evidence of adverse effects of the introduction of a LLM on employment outcomes, we turn to explore the heterogeneity in treatment effects in order to shed light on the drivers of the main estimates.

st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central distinction between task-performance equalization and labour-market rewards. In exposed Upwork occupations, employment and earnings declined, while the authors also interpreted heterogeneous effects as potentially narrowing productivity gaps. Its short horizon and platform-specific setting limit generalization but do not alter that supportive direction.

st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between task-level capability and broader labor-market outcomes. kp.k: Upwork provides early evidence of generative AI employment effects
kp.d: Hui, Reshef and Zhou examine freelance employment rather than legal services specifically. Although the supplied heading identifies a 2024 Organization Science article, the reproduced text is CESifo Working Paper No. 10601, August 2023. Its analysis covers January 2022 through April 2023, using publicly available Upwork employment histories aggregated by job-start month. The text reports 92,547 freelancers, whereas Table 1 reports 92,457; these are inconsistent sample counts in the supplied document. The sample is restricted to freelancers offering a single occupation, approximately 85% of freelancers.
qs: We restrict our attention to the period from January 2022 through April 2023.
Our final data set consists of 92,547 freelancers.
Employment outcomes are aggregated to the freelancer-month level by the date at which the job started, focusing on monthly number of jobs and monthly income.

kp.k: Exposure design compares writing occupations with less-affected freelancers
kp.d: The authors use ChatGPT's November 30, 2022 release as a shock to AI accessibility and salience. Their difference-in-differences design compares writing, proofreading and copy-editing occupations with less-affected occupations, incorporating freelancer and month fixed effects and occupation-clustered standard errors. They justify writing exposure through existing task-exposure research, text-generation capabilities, media coverage and descriptive Google Trends evidence. These exposure indicators are not direct observations of freelancers' or buyers' AI adoption.
qs: The release of ChatGPT3 on November 30, 2022
provides a shock to both the salience and accessi- bility of generative AI and LLMs.
All regressions also include freelancer and month fixed effects.

The key identifying assumption of the difference-in-differences design is that freelancers operating in more affected and less affected occupations would have evolved similarly, absent the release of GPT.

kp.k: Exposed freelancers experienced lower monthly jobs and earnings
kp.d: Relative to less-affected occupations, the authors report a 2% reduction in monthly jobs and a 5.2% reduction in monthly earnings following ChatGPT's release, both statistically significant at the 1% level. Table 2 reports coefficients of -0.020 (standard error 0.004) and -0.052 (0.016), respectively, using 1,236,052 freelancer-month observations and 195 occupation clusters. The narrative describes logged outcomes and percentage effects, but Table 2 specifies inverse hyperbolic sine transformations.
qs: Following the release, the monthly number of jobs on the platform for free- lancers in more affected occupations decreases by 2% (s.e.=0.004), and total monthly compensation decreases by 5.2% (s.e.=0.016).
In columns 1, 2, 4, and 5, the dependent variables are inverse hyperbolic sine transformed.

kp.k: Losses occur through both employment probability and job volume
kp.d: The probability of starting at least one job in a month falls by 1.2 percentage points, approximately 10% relative to baseline employment. Conditional on obtaining work, monthly jobs fall by approximately 4.7% (standard error 0.011). Conditional monthly income falls by approximately 5.1%, but this estimate is not statistically significant; its standard error is 0.037 in the narrative and 0.033 in Table 2. The detailed results clarify that the extensive-margin effect is percentage points, despite percentage wording in the introduction.
qs: Following the release of GPT, the probability that a freelancer offering writing-related services starts a new job in a given month decreases by 1.2 percentage points, which is approximately a 10% drop compared to baseline employment.

The number of jobs decreases by approximately 4.7% (s.e.=0.011), which is substantially larger than the total effect, and the effect of income is approximately the same size, a decrease of 5.1%, though it is much noisier (s.e.=0.037).

kp.k: Pre-trends and robustness checks support the authors' causal interpretation
kp.d: The event study shows similar pre-release trends and a persistent, growing post-release decline in jobs and compensation, which the authors interpret as supporting parallel trends and a causal relationship. They report robustness to alternative controls, wild-bootstrap inference, industry-level clustering and coarsened exact matching on prior employment, income, education, badges, success rate and hourly rate. The matching exercise reportedly strengthens results and improves precision; these checks do not remove the design's stated identifying assumption.
qs: Reassuringly, we observe similar pre-trends between freelancers in eventually treated and untreated occupations prior to the release of ChatGPT, which provides suggestive evidence in favor of the parallel trends assumption.
Following its release, we see a persistent and growing decrease in both the monthly number of jobs (Panel A) and monthly compensation (Panel B) on the platform, suggesting a causal relationship.
using the matched sample improves the precision of, and generally strengthens, the main results.

kp.k: Image-generation releases show similar adverse freelance outcomes
kp.d: An additional analysis treats design, image editing and art services as exposed to DALL-E 2 and Midjourney. The detailed account dates DALL-E 2's release to April 2022 and Midjourney's to July, coding the post-treatment period as post-April 2022. The authors report qualitatively similar negative effects on job numbers and compensation, presenting this as evidence supporting the design and broader applicability across freelance domains. The cited appendix tables are not reproduced in the supplied text.
qs: Both models were released at about the same time, with DALL-E 2 released in April 2022, and Midjourney in July.
To be conservative, we code the post period as post-April 2022.
we find consistent negative effects of the release of the new technology on the performance of freelancers on the platform, in terms of both number of jobs and total compensation.

kp.k: Past quality does not reliably protect exposed freelancers
kp.d: The authors test heterogeneity using past jobs, earnings, buyer-required experience level, top-rated badges, success rates and stated hourly rates. They find no evidence that higher measured quality cushions employment losses, and suggest that top freelancers may suffer more. Many interaction estimates, particularly for income, are not statistically significant. For above-median prior earnings, the narrative reports additional writing-related reductions of 1.2% in jobs and 2.9% in income, with the latter insignificant; corresponding image-service reductions are 7% and 14%, both significant at 1%. These are platform-based quality proxies, not direct measures of general ability.
qs: In general, across the various measures of freelancers’ quality, we can generally rule out that freelancers’ quality moderates the adverse employment effects of generative AI.
These effect, however, are often not statistically significant, especially for monthly income, which tends to be substantially noisier.
For image-based services, we estimate re- ductions of 7% and 14% for freelancers with above median prior earnings, both significant at the 1% level.

kp.k: Substitution and narrowing skill gaps are interpretations, not measurements
kp.d: The authors interpret employment and earnings declines as short-term substitution for knowledge workers across quality levels. They interpret heterogeneous effects through a skill-biased technological change framework, conditional on relatively stable short-run labor supply, as consistent with narrowing productivity gaps. Experimental findings that AI disproportionately improves lower-ability workers' performance are cited from other studies, not established through this paper's own productivity measurement. They acknowledge that their outcomes concern relative earnings rather than relative wages.
qs: We interpret these findings as suggesting that generative AI models act as a substitute for knowledge workers of all quality types, at least in the short term, effectively reducing their employment and earnings.
The heterogeneous effects are consistent with generative AI potentially reducing the pro- ductivity gap between low-quality and high-quality workers.
Although our results, technically speaking, concern changes in the relative earnings rather than relative wages, the qualitative insight is similar.

kp.k: Platform coverage limits conclusions about total employment and skill
kp.d: The study does not observe off-platform employment, so platform losses cannot establish total employment losses rather than shifts elsewhere. Data cover searchable freelancers with active profiles in April 2023, excluding terminated accounts and an unknown share of non-searchable workers. Profiles are a single snapshot, preventing observation of changes in qualifications and certain quality indicators; badges, success rates and hourly rates are observed at collection rather than necessarily before treatment. The authors also cannot establish whether highly skilled Upwork workers are highly skilled in the wider population.
qs: Notably, we are only able to observe a snapshot of the freelancer pool as it was in April 2023, and are unable to observe changes made in the profile page over time.
our sample only includes freelancers with active profiles at the time of obtaining the data, as we do not observe terminated accounts.
we are unable to evaluate whether high-skills Upwork workers are also highly skilled in the general population.

kp.k: Flexible spot markets reveal effects before traditional employment
kp.d: The authors argue that Upwork's short-term projects and frequent opportunities to renegotiate and rehire make it especially suitable for detecting immediate AI effects. This is a setting-based explanation for early observable changes, not evidence that equivalent effects already occur in permanent employment or legal practice.
qs: Due to the flexibility of this spot market compared to traditional, formal employment, it is a great setting to explore the short-term effects of ChatGPT.
Thus, while LLMs are still too young to replace full-time jobs, we may already be able to detect its effect in an online labor market.

kp.k: Long-term complementarity and overall welfare remain unresolved
kp.d: The authors characterize the findings as preliminary short-term evidence. They identify competing longer-term possibilities: broader adoption could worsen labor losses, while integration with other tools could increasingly complement workers. They recommend further scrutiny by policymakers and business leaders and careful examination of adaptation and adoption, warning that past performance may not preserve competitive advantage. They explicitly do not assess total welfare across stakeholders.
qs: However, the long-term implications may be significantly different, and it is unclear how our findings extend to longer time horizons.
In contrast, as the development of AI capabilities continues it may become more integrated with various tools and begin to better complement the performance of human workers.
Assessing the total welfare implications to the introduction of generative AI technology to all stakeholders is beyond the scope of this paper and remains a promising direction for future work.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Hui, Reshef and Zhou report short-term reductions in Upwork employment and earnings following generative AI releases, with no evidence that higher-quality service protects freelancers.
pts.d: In the supplied 2023 working-paper text, the authors report that writing-related freelancers experienced approximately 2% fewer monthly jobs and 5.2% lower monthly earnings relative to less-affected occupations after ChatGPT's release. The probability of starting any new job fell by 1.2 percentage points, approximately 10% relative to baseline; among those receiving work, jobs fell by approximately 4.7%. Conditional earnings fell by an estimated 5.1%, but that estimate was not statistically significant. The authors report qualitatively similar adverse effects for design and image-related freelancers after image-generation model releases. They interpret the findings as short-term substitution for knowledge workers, rather than protection through high-quality service. Evidence that top freelancers were disproportionately affected is described as suggestive, especially for writing-related earnings. They also suggest that AI could narrow productivity gaps between workers; this is an interpretation, not a directly measured productivity result.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on observational freelancer histories and difference-in-differences estimates, supported by event studies and robustness analyses.
pts.d: The authors use Upwork API records aggregated to freelancer-month outcomes, comparing writing, proofreading and copy-editing with less-affected occupations before and after ChatGPT's launch. The narrative reports 92,547 freelancers, while Table 1 reports 92,457. Regressions include freelancer and month fixed effects, time-varying controls and occupation-clustered standard errors. Table 2 identifies the job and income outcomes as inverse-hyperbolic-sine transformed, although the narrative describes them as logged and interprets coefficients as approximate percentage changes. Both headline estimates are significant at the 1% level. Supporting analyses include event-study pre-trends, alternative controls and clustering, wild bootstrap inference, matched samples and an analogous image-generation analysis. Occupational exposure research and Google Trends motivate the treatment classification, rather than measure actual AI adoption. Quality heterogeneity is assessed using previous jobs, earnings, required experience, badges, success rates and hourly rates. Some heterogeneity estimates are not statistically significant; badges, success rates and hourly rates are observed only at the April 2023 collection date. The supplied excerpt discusses appendices but does not reproduce their tables.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The authors restrict their findings to immediate and short-term platform outcomes and explicitly leave long-term effects unresolved.
pts.d: The data cover January 2022–April 2023, with ChatGPT treatment beginning after November 2022. The image-model analysis codes the post-period as after April 2022, noting DALL-E 2's April release and Midjourney's July release. The authors argue that a flexible, short-project market can reveal effects earlier than conventional full-time employment. Their causal interpretation depends on parallel trends. Off-platform work is unobserved, so platform losses need not equal total employment losses. Sampling captures only searchable profiles active at collection, excluding terminated accounts and historical profile changes. The interpretation of relative worker outcomes through a skill-biased technological-change model assumes that short-run Upwork labor supply does not change dramatically. Longer-term displacement could deepen with diffusion, but improved integration could instead increase complementarity. Total welfare effects are outside the study's scope.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly studied population is Upwork freelancers in text- and image-related services, not lawyers or legal-service organisations.
pts.d: The primary affected group comprises freelancers offering writing, proofreading and copy-editing; the secondary analysis concerns design, image editing and art. Outcomes concern new projects and earnings on Upwork, rather than full-time job losses or economy-wide unemployment. The main sample is restricted to single-occupation freelancers, approximately 85% of freelancers according to the authors. Across measures of past performance and experience, higher-quality freelancers are not found to be insulated, and some estimates suggest greater losses among them. The authors draw broader implications for business leaders and incumbent competitive advantage, but these extend beyond the directly observed platform outcomes. This is a cross-domain labor-market source and provides no legal-sector-specific employment estimate or prediction.
